questions.prompt: A deploy job must wait for a test job to succeed. Which workflow field establishes that dependency?

choices.text: A test-job output reference without declaring a needs dependency.
needs on the deploy job.
The order of job names in the YAML file alone.
A longer test timeout without configuring a deployment dependency.

questions.explanation: needs declares a dependency. YAML presentation order, step names and variable labels do not impose job ordering.

sources.title: GitHub Actions workflow syntax
sources.claim: GitHub Actions jobs can run in parallel by default; needs establishes dependencies and skipped or failed prerequisites normally prevent dependent jobs.

questions.prompt: A build job produces a bundle required by a deploy job. What should transfer that output?

choices.text: Upload and download the bundle as an artifact.
Assume another runner can read the build runner’s local disk.
Use only a dependency-cache hit as proof the bundle exists.
Assume a dependency cache always contains the exact output of the current build.

questions.explanation: Artifacts transfer generated files across job boundaries. Separate runners do not share their local filesystem by default, and caches serve a different purpose.

sources.title: Storing workflow data as artifacts
sources.claim: Workflow artifacts persist files for sharing between jobs or after a run; caches are intended to speed reuse of dependencies rather than replace build deliverables.

questions.prompt: A job sets contents: read under permissions. What happens to omitted permission scopes?

choices.text: They all become write by default.
They retain all repository defaults despite the explicit permissions map.
They all receive the same read grant regardless of scope.
They are set to none.

questions.explanation: Specifying permissions sets omitted scopes to none, overriding inherited defaults for those scopes. A read grant applies only to the named scope and does not grant all-scope read or write access.

sources.title: GitHub Actions workflow syntax
sources.claim: GitHub Actions permissions can be constrained per workflow or job; when specified, omitted scopes are set to none.

questions.prompt: A deploy job references an environment with required approval. When may it access that environment’s secrets?

choices.text: Before approval so it can bypass the environment gate.
Whenever deployment starts on a runner, even while approval is pending.
After its environment protection rules are satisfied.
As soon as any unrelated test job starts.

questions.explanation: Environment protection gates execution and access to its secrets. Other jobs and naming conventions do not satisfy the gate.

sources.title: Managing environments for deployment
sources.claim: A job referencing a protected environment must meet its rules before running or accessing environment secrets; feature availability depends on repository and plan.

questions.prompt: A workflow lists build, test and deploy as separate jobs with no dependencies. Which assumption is unsafe?

choices.text: That a deploy dependency should name its required test job.
That file order makes deploy wait for the tests.
That needs can explicitly connect dependent jobs.
That independent jobs may be scheduled concurrently.

questions.explanation: YAML listing order is not scheduling order. Explicit needs is required for the desired dependency graph.

sources.title: GitHub Actions workflow syntax
sources.claim: needs declares successful prerequisite jobs instead of relying on YAML order.

questions.prompt: A deploy job downloads a bundle before its producing build job has finished. What additional coordination is needed?

choices.text: Make deploy depend on the producing build job.
Assume download automatically schedules every required build.
Assume artifact retention settings create a dependency on the current build.
Put deploy below build in YAML without declaring a needs dependency.

questions.explanation: The consumer needs the artifact after production. A job dependency supplies ordering; names do not and downloading is not a build scheduler.

sources.title: Storing workflow data as artifacts
sources.claim: Artifacts carry generated files across jobs; a producing job should precede its consumer.

questions.prompt: Which GitHub Actions job-order statements hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A step name automatically creates a dependency between different jobs.
Jobs can run in parallel unless dependencies constrain them.
needs identifies jobs that must complete before a dependent job.
Listing deploy below test guarantees a successful test prerequisite.
A dependent job always runs after a failed prerequisite without any condition.

questions.explanation: A is incorrect: Job dependencies use needs, not display names. B is correct: Independent jobs need not follow file order. C is correct: It forms explicit dependency relationships. D is incorrect: Presentation order does not declare dependencies. E is incorrect: Failure normally prevents dependent execution.

sources.title: GitHub Actions workflow syntax
sources.claim: GitHub Actions jobs can run in parallel by default; needs establishes dependencies and skipped or failed prerequisites normally prevent dependent jobs.

questions.prompt: Which artifact practices fit a multi-job workflow? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Upload generated output that another job needs.
Download the expected artifact in the consuming job.
Configure retention for stored artifacts where appropriate.
Assume all hosted jobs share one permanent filesystem.
Treat a dependency cache as identical to a published build deliverable.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Artifacts persist files beyond the producing job. B is correct: The files must be retrieved into that job’s environment. C is correct: Artifacts have a storage lifecycle. D is incorrect: Jobs can run on separate runners. E is incorrect: Caches optimize reuse; artifacts persist outputs and evidence.

sources.title: Storing workflow data as artifacts
sources.claim: Workflow artifacts persist files for sharing between jobs or after a run; caches are intended to speed reuse of dependencies rather than replace build deliverables.

questions.prompt: Which token-permission practices fit least privilege? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Use job-level permissions when jobs need different access.
Assume a read grant on one scope implies writes on every other scope.
Set write-all merely to avoid understanding deployment requirements.
Assume all scopes become writable when any one scope receives read access.
Grant only the scopes required by the job.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Permissions can be scoped to individual jobs. B is incorrect: Each scope has independent access. C is incorrect: Broad write grants are unnecessary when narrower scopes suffice. D is incorrect: Access is controlled by permission configuration. E is correct: Unneeded access increases the impact of compromised workflow code.

sources.title: GitHub Actions workflow syntax
sources.claim: GitHub Actions permissions can be constrained per workflow or job; when specified, omitted scopes are set to none.

questions.prompt: Which deployment-environment statements are appropriate? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Verify rule availability for the repository visibility and plan.
Environment secrets are unconditionally available before its protection rules pass.
Naming a branch production automatically applies every environment rule.
Reference the environment from the deployment job.
Configure relevant deployment protection rules where available.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Not every feature is available on every plan. B is incorrect: Access is gated by those rules. C is incorrect: Environment association is configured on the job. D is correct: The job must name it to use its configuration. E is correct: Rules can constrain deployment execution.

sources.title: Managing environments for deployment
sources.claim: A job referencing a protected environment must meet its rules before running or accessing environment secrets; feature availability depends on repository and plan.
